docs.title: Where do language models belong in this pipeline, and where not?
The answer
docs.text: In four places, measured, and not in two others. A model reads a flagged call site in source code, classifies an algorithm against a policy, and drafts the change that would alter a listener's posture — a 31B model on the lab's four L4s does all three, the first with its reasoning mode on, and drafts the plan better and far faster than the largest model the lab holds. A model traces a finding on the wire to the configuration line that produces it — that is the one role that needs a 120B model. A model does not decide whether a change worked; the verifier is a pair of probes. And two roles the design first gave to a model go back to rules: naming a tool's spelling, which is a table lookup, and resolving a conflict between findings, which no arm of fifteen did within the harm allowed. These are measurements on 216 labeled items with a floor per role written before any run, across three rounds and every model the lab holds, not opinions about what models can do.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Rules, parsers and scanners first; a model only where interpretation is needed. That is the project's rule, and the question it leaves open is where interpretation is actually needed — and which model, since the lab's models live on different machines with different costs: a 30B engine resident beside the 120B on a desk-side box, a 31B model on four data-centre GPUs, a second host that serves one model at a time. Spike S3 answers it the way the rest of the project answers things: a labeled set per role, a floor per role below which the output cannot be used as designed, a threshold written down before anything ran, and a verifier, not a reader, scoring the role whose output can be verified.

A floor matters more than a comparison. A model that beats another is not thereby good enough; a role whose output goes into the inventory unchecked needs near-perfect accuracy, and a role whose output is rehearsed and verified before anything depends on it can tolerate less. Once several arms clear a floor, the cheapest by latency is bound.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
Six roles, one prompt each, the same prompt for every arm, a JSON schema on every reply so that scoring compares fields, and three calls per item with the majority taken. Round 1 compared the two engines the lab had bound to its tiers; rounds 2 and 3 ran every other model the lab holds, and a successor to the 120B, on the same items against the same floors. The floors, what each role's reply is checked against, and where each role landed:

Role Reply checked against Floor (harmful allowed) Bound to Measured The nearest other arms Call-site read A label with the quoted line and what in it decides each field 27 (1) Gemma 4 31B on four L4s, reasoning on 29 of 30, 13.6 s 120B 29 at 42 s; 30B with reasoning 28 at 84 s; 30B alone 21 Normalization RFCs, the IANA registries, OIDs 28 (0) rules: a name table; the live lab/reason as fallback since 2026-10-21 28 with none harmful, 9.8 s (round 5), the only arm at the floor best before 27, four arms; a fallback reply is shown as unconfirmed Classification The memo's own table of quantum-vulnerable algorithms 28 (0) Gemma 4 31B on four L4s, no reasoning 30 of 30, 1.1 s five arms at 30; 30B alone 25 Conflict resolution What the wire showed when the configuration was started 24 of 29 (2) rules decide; the live lab/reason explains beside them since 2026-10-21 26 with 2 harmful, 41 s (round 5, the live lane), the first arm at the floor; 10 of 29 items unstable 23 with 4 harmful for the same model through the bake-off's lane; Gemma 31B with reasoning 21; 30B alone 1, with 13 harmful Trace to cause The line whose change made the finding go 24 (3) deliberate on the lab GB10: Nemotron 3 Super 120B with full thinking until 2026-10-19, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B at medium effort since 28 of 30 on both the old engine's runs, 36 to 44 s; 27 of 30 on the live lane after the change, 12.7 s Super VL at medium effort 26 (2 harmful); GPT-OSS 120B 26 but 4 harmful; Gemma 31B 22 with reasoning; 30B 9 Change plan The plan applied in a lab and probed by the verifier 24 (2) Gemma 4 31B on four L4s, no reasoning 27 of 30, none harmful, 3.5 s 120B 24 to 25 with 1 harmful at 95 s; Super VL thinking off 24 with 2 harmful; Gemma 31B with reasoning on the second host 24 with 1 at 75 s

The binding rule: a role goes to the cheapest arm, by median latency, that reaches the floor with no more harmful answers than the role allows; a role no arm reaches stays a rule's job. "Harmful" is a wrong answer that would cause damage as designed: a plan that takes the service down, a definite layer named where the evidence cannot tell. Round 1's stricter test for "needs the larger model" — the small engine below the floor, the large one above it, and at least five discordant pairs at p ≤ 0.05 on an exact sign test — is what first separated the trace role from the rest.

Three measurements the rule does not score and a design must:

  • Temperature 0 is not determinism. The 120B gave different replies to the same prompt on 57 of 178 items, the thinking engine on 50. Majority of three makes the counts above stable; a single call is not.
  • A wrong change plan usually fails by taking the service down. Of 119 distinct plans run in the lab across round 1's arms, 32 left the service not listening and 6 landed a change that did not take. That is the argument for rehearsal in a twin and for an applier that restores the previous file when the service does not come up.
  • The reasoning setting moves a result more than a change of model. The 120B's successor, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, loaded in the same slot, traced 9 of 30 findings with thinking off, 26 at medium effort and 21 at full thinking with a quarter of its long calls timing out; the two 120B models at the same setting differed by two (lesson 26). The incumbent's two runs nine days apart differed by about two items per role, which is the spike's noise.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The trace-to-cause role, where the models differ most. One item: OpenSSH 10 with KexAlgorithms set twice in sshd_config, the first line listing curve25519-sha256,ecdh-sha2-nistp256 and a later line, after a "hardening pass" comment, listing diffie-hellman-group14-sha256. The wire finding is that the listener offers ecdh-sha2-nistp256. OpenSSH takes the first value it reads, so the cause is line 4; the label was confirmed by changing that line and watching the finding go (lesson 19). The small engine answered default — no line sets it — on this and on most items; the 120B named line 4. Across the thirty items, which also turn on include order in OpenSSH, last-value-wins in PostgreSQL and innermost-block-wins in nginx (lesson 20), the 120B was right on 28 and the small engine on 9, and no model under 120B parameters passed 22.

The change-plan role, where the number to read is the other one. The item is an nginx server with a classical curve line in an included snippet, and the intent require. A correct plan edits the snippet to ssl_protocols TLSv1.3; and ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768;; the verifier then finds the hybrid-only client accepted and the classical-only client refused: enforced. The plans that failed did not mostly leave the service classical; they wrote a line nginx would not load, and the service never listened. The 31B model on the L4s wrote no such plan in 30 items; the 120B wrote one, and Llama 3.3 70B on the second host wrote fourteen.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
• Bind roles to tiers from the measurement, with the reasoning setting. The inference seam binds each role to a tier and a reasoning flag in its configuration file; code never chooses a model for a role, and a role no arm reached is left unbound and is a rule's job. Today fast is the 31B model on the L4s and deliberate the 120B on the lab GB10.
  • One role needs the big machine. The trace is answered inline at the 120B's own latency, a median of 13 s on the engine serving today. Everything else a model does here runs on four L4s at a few seconds a call, and a person asking "why is this listener classical" gets the rule's answer at once either way.
  • Measure a successor against the floor before it takes the slot, and again on the live lane after it has. A newer model of the same size in the same slot was not a step up for this work; at its medium reasoning effort it clears the one floor the slot serves, two items under the incumbent, and with thinking off it does not. The lab's slot changed to it on 2026-10-19, at medium effort, for the sake of its other callers; the one role this project binds there was re-measured on the live lane the next day: 27 of 30 with 2 harmful at 12.7 s a call, one item under the old engine and within the noise, so the binding stands (spike S3 round 4). A slot that serves several callers is bound to one reasoning setting, and the setting is part of what was measured.
  • Conflict resolution is a rule's job, and is built as one. The rule conflict/resolve/1 settles each disagreement between a file in an image and what the wire shows from evidence the ledger already holds — not-served, tool-limit, or cannot-tell with what is missing named — in the vocabulary the spike labelled. On the eight-service estate it settled all three conflicts present with no model call. A deployment that binds the resolve-conflict role may have a model explain each conflict beside the rule's answer; the explanation is recorded as the model's, marked unused by any rule, and never settles one. The lab binds no model to the role.
  • The investigator's loop runs on the bound engine at about half a minute a finding. The trace role, measured as one call with every file handed over, now runs as a loop: the model reads, greps and answers over the service's build files through three typed tools under a step budget of 8 and a token budget of 60,000, with no shell. On the first run over the eight-service estate it traced nine findings, one per listener, in two to four steps and 1,800 to 6,400 tokens each, a median of 27.6 s and a range of 23 to 89 s on the live lane; eight agreed with the answer key's cause and the ninth disagreed because the key was wrong (lesson 31). Every trace is recorded as the model's claim with the engine, the settings, each step and the measured time; no rule, link or verdict reads it. One trace repeated twice shows why a single call is not a measurement (lesson 21): with a 4,000-token cap per reply the engine's thinking on one step ran 232 s and the next reply came back empty, no answer after 449 s; with the cap at 16,000, as the spike ran the single call, the same finding was answered in two steps and 44.9 s. On a lane that thinks, the reply cap bounds the thinking too, and a cap that fits a terse answer starves the step that needed to deliberate (lesson 26).
  • A seventh role was tried and is not bound. Explaining, in plain words, why a migration item sits in its queue — over passages of the policy pack that an embedding retrieved — was given a floor before its first call and reached 3 of 14 items on Gemma 4 31B, with 3 harmful answers. The model was not the limit: retrieval missed the passage naming the item's queue in 11 of 14, and where it was retrieved the model passed every call (lesson 34). The page shows the rule's own basis instead.
  • A new engine was measured on every role, on the lane as it serves. Round 5 ran Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on the live lab/reason lane on the five roles round 4 left. Two roles no arm had reached now reach their floor there — normalization at 28 with none harmful, conflict resolution at 26 with 2 — and neither changes who decides: the name table and the conflict rule still do, and the model is the fallback and the explainer. Change plans fell to 19 with 4 harmful, and stay on Gemma 31B. The same model and setting scored differently through the bake-off's lane and the live one (lesson 26).
  • Never act on a single reply. Repeat, verify, or use a rule.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Covered: six roles, 30 scored items each (29 for conflict resolution), fifteen arms through the lab gateway between 2026-10-07 and 2026-10-20: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B with and without reasoning and Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B on the lab GB10; Gemma 4 31B FP8 with and without reasoning on the xr7620's four L4s; on a second host through ollama, Gemma 4 31B q8 with and without reasoning (the thinking arm's last three roles completed on 2026-10-20 after two refused-connection losses), GPT-OSS 120B, Llama 3.3 70B and Lightning; Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B in the 120B's slot with thinking on, at medium effort and off, beside the incumbent re-run the same day. Labels checked by a second reader; threshold and items committed before the first run.

Not covered: GPT-OSS 120B and Llama 70B under vLLM on the GB10, which would evict the deliberate engine; prompts tuned beyond six development items per role; the embed tier. The investigator's loop has run once, on nine findings of the planted estate, and is a measurement of that engine on those files, not a second spike: no other arm has run the loop, and nine is not thirty. A floor of 24 or 28 on 30 items is a coarse instrument, and the incumbent's two runs show the noise is about two items; a role within two of its floor could land on the other side on another draw.

docs.title: What do the open-source scanners cover, and what is built on top?
The answer
docs.text: Run together, three open-source tools produce most of a first cryptographic inventory for network listeners and container images: testssl.sh for TLS, ssh-audit for SSH, and cbomkit-theia for certificates and keys inside images. On the four-service slice they find 22 of 23 items on the wire and 7 of 10 in images; on the eight-service estate, 38 of 40 and 14 of 20, the two wire misses being keyed out of reach. A harness built on top of them finds the same wire items. What it adds is in the images and in the structure: its own reader of key material finds what theia cannot read — an ML-DSA certificate and its key, a PKCS#12 keystore, DSA and Ed25519 host keys — and its rules say which wire finding and which file are the same key, which certificate in an image is not served by anything (while leaving a certificate authority's alone), and what each listener's posture is. On the estate that is 20 of 20 image items against 14, two decoys avoided against two flagged, and nine postures stated against none.

docs.title: The concept: three layers, three kinds of tool
docs.text:
A cryptography bill of materials (CBOM) is an inventory of cryptographic assets: algorithms, keys, certificates, protocols, each with where it was found. Evidence for it comes from three layers:

Layer What is observed Tool here Wire What a listener negotiates when a client connects testssl.sh (TLS), ssh-audit (SSH) Host Files in an image or on a disk: certificates, keys, configuration cbomkit-theia Code Calls to cryptographic libraries in source CBOMkit's source scanners (Java, Python, Go) — not yet run in this project

No single tool spans the layers. CBOMkit, the open-source CBOM toolset, does not scan networks, so against a wire-only estate it scores zero by construction. That makes "better than CBOMkit" an empty comparison for anything that includes a network scanner. The comparison that means something is against all the scanners run together with no harness.

docs.title: The mechanism: how the comparison is made fair
docs.text:
An answer key lists what a perfect inventory holds. Each item has a class: present (planted, findable), decoy (looks like a finding, is not), out-of-reach (real, but no scan can see it) or supplied (can only be typed in). Out-of-reach items stay in the denominator and are reported as known misses. A reported decoy is a false positive. So is a claim, on a keyed listener, of a key-establishment or signature algorithm the key does not hold.

Three inventories are scored from one scan:

  • CBOMkit alone — cbomkit-theia's findings only.
  • Scanners alone — every tool's findings, unioned, with names normalized and duplicates folded, and nothing else.
  • Workbench — the same findings plus the output of three rules.

Both baselines pass through the same normalizer as the workbench, so they are scored on what the tools said in one vocabulary. That is generous to the baselines: name normalization and de-duplication are credited to them.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The estate: two TLS listeners (one classical, one offering a hybrid group) and two SSH listeners (OpenSSH 6.6 and OpenSSH 10.0), with their four images. Measured 2026-10-03 on an x86_64 lab server.

Layer CBOMkit alone Scanners alone Workbench Wire, of 23 0 22 22 Host, of 10 7 7 7 Host decoy flagged yes yes no Listener posture, of 4 not stated not stated 4

What the scanners got right. Both wire tools report post-quantum hybrids by name: testssl.sh lists X25519MLKEM768 under its KEM line, and ssh-audit lists mlkem768x25519-sha256 and sntrup761x25519-sha512. Every classical key-exchange group and every host-key type on all four listeners was found.

What they missed, and why.

Miss Layer Reason What the legacy SFTP server offers when it connects out Wire No listener shows it; only traffic capture beside the client would. Keyed as out-of-reach DSA host key file Host cbomkit-theia reports it as "private-key" with no algorithm. The workbench does not guess one Two Ed25519 host key files Host cbomkit-theia 1.1.2 reported neither; both are in OpenSSH's own key format

The decoy. One image holds a second certificate, RSA-1024 with SHA-1, that no listener serves. cbomkit-theia reports it identically to the served certificate, as it should: it reads files. The workbench compares the public key of each certificate served on the wire with each certificate found in the image, links the ones that match, and marks the unmatched one, and everything read from that file, as not in use. It makes that judgement only when every listener of that image was scanned and each served certificate was found in the image; otherwise it says nothing.

What the rules add.

Rule Adds Link by public key "The certificate at 172.16.106.10:443 is the file /etc/nginx/tls/portal.crt in this image" — the first link of a dependency chain, with the hash as evidence In use or not Separates what an image contains from what a service uses Posture Per listener: classical, mixed (post-quantum key exchange, classical authentication) or post-quantum

Cost. A targeted TLS scan takes 27 to 46 s per listener; SSH takes 2 to 3 s. An image scan takes 71 to 96 s for images of a few megabytes, nearly all of it in cbomkit-theia's secrets plugin, which reads a file once for every symlink that points to it — Alpine's BusyBox has 304 (lesson 09). Image contents change only when an image does, so those results are replayed from the ledger with their original timestamps, and a routine re-scan takes as long as its slowest TLS listener.

The baseline is the tool's own document. Scored with no normalizer at all, cbomkit-theia's own CBOM files give the same 7 of 10 and the same flagged decoy as the projected baseline — once a reader follows theia's own reference from a certificate to its key. Read by component name alone they give 5 of 10, because theia names a certificate by its subject, not its algorithm.

docs.title: Beyond the slice: what each scanner can see
docs.text:
A second set of targets was built to ask the questions the slice does not: a TLS 1.3 server with an ML-DSA-65 certificate, Postgres 18 over its in-protocol TLS upgrade, RabbitMQ 4 and Kafka 4.1 over TLS, a listener that demands a client certificate, a client watched passively by Zeek, and one Ruby call site. Each tool ran on x86_64 and again as arm64 under emulation.

Capability testssl.sh OpenSSL sweep ssh-audit cbomkit-theia Zeek Opengrep Hybrid told from classical, TLS yes yes — — yes (x86_64) — Hybrid told from classical, SSH — — yes — — — ML-DSA-65 certificate yes, on the wire yes, on the wire — no: drops the file — — Postgres over its TLS upgrade yes yes — — — — RabbitMQ, Kafka over TLS yes yes — — — — Client-certificate listener yes yes — — — — A client's offered groups — — — — yes (x86_64) — A Ruby call site — — — — — yes, one rule

The open-source wire tools are further along than expected: testssl.sh reads an ML-DSA certificate even though its own bundled OpenSSL predates ML-DSA. The weak point is the file layer. Neither broker offered any post-quantum group, so on those images a hybrid requirement cannot be configured at all — a migration fact, not a scanner gap.

Two limits of this table. A list of accepted groups is not the whole of key establishment: in TLS 1.2 a server may also accept RSA key transport, where the client encrypts the session secret to the server's RSA key and no group is involved. The Postgres target, configured with the hybrid group and X25519, still accepts it. A scan that reports groups reports that server as "hybrid and X25519"; anyone recording its traffic needs only the server's RSA key, later. An inventory of key establishment on a TLS 1.2 listener needs the cipher suites as well as the groups. The harness's TLS scan therefore asks testssl.sh for every cipher suite as well (-E), which costs 9 to 17 s more per listener on the slice, and reports each TLS_RSA_WITH_* suite as key establishment by RSA. On the slice's portal — an RSA certificate, TLS 1.2 allowed, only ECDHE suites configured — it correctly reports none; that listener is the answer key's wire decoy for exactly this inference. And a "yes" in the table means the two wire tools agree with each other and with what the target was configured to offer; for the two brokers, whose group lists are their runtimes' defaults, it means the tools agree. A server's own account is not a third witness: RabbitMQ lists three Brainpool TLS 1.3 groups it then refuses on the wire.

Three times testssl.sh looked wrong and the reference was wrong instead (lesson 10): a comparison of scanners is only as good as its reference probe.

docs.title: Other open-source tools, tried and not adopted
docs.text:
Three more free tools were tried on the same terms — pinned image, run on the workbench's networks or offline, judged against what they should find:

Tool What it should find What it did Decision sslyze 6.2.0 the groups each TLS listener accepts lists no post-quantum group; reports a hybrid-only listener as no TLS at all; reported secp256r1 rejected where a direct P-256 handshake completed not adopted for key establishment; testssl.sh stays, and the second witness stays OpenSSL 3.5 probes cdxgen 11.11.0, CBOM mode crypto call sites in Java and Python none, offline, in either pinned repository not adopted: needs a build and the network sonar-cryptography 1.6.1 (CBOMkit) in SonarQube crypto call sites in Java, Python, Go none: Python coverage is pyca/cryptography only, which the Python repository does not use; Java needs compiled classes not adopted while third-party repositories are never built; the right tool for a team scanning its own built code

The pattern is the one a reader should test for in any tool: silence is not a finding until the tool has been shown something it should report. All three were silent where the planted or labelled material says otherwise.

docs.title: Any tool's CBOM, scored
docs.text: Federal agencies inventory with commercial discovery tools. Rather than pick among them, the workbench imports any tool's CycloneDX CBOM as evidence (pqch import): each entry is placed on a scoped listener, a file in a named image or a call site in a pinned repository, named the way the workbench names its own, and scored against the answer key. Entries the importer cannot place — the CycloneDX project's own CBOM examples have no locations — are kept in the import's record by name and not counted. cbomkit-theia's own CBOMs, imported this way, score exactly what its native reader scores.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
• Start with the free scanners. For listeners and images they give most of an Enumerated-rung inventory with no harness at all.
  • Expect noise at the host layer. This estate's images had their system trust stores removed so the key could be exact. The base images they are built from carry 148 (Ubuntu 14.04) and 121 (Alpine 3.22) certificate-authority certificates, and a file scanner reports every one. Telling "contains" from "uses" is the first real problem there.
  • Check each scanner against a known target before trusting an absence. A tool that does not parse one key format reports nothing, which reads the same as "none present".
  • State the delta honestly. At this rung a harness earns its place by structure and by what it enables next — tracing, prioritizing, verifying a change — not by finding more.

docs.title: What the harness adds at M1: its own reader of files
docs.text: cbomkit-theia stays the candidate generator and the baseline for the image layer. Beside it the runner runs the harness's own reader (pqch image-files) from its own image, with no network, over the same archive: it walks the image's layers, honouring whiteouts, reads PEM and DER certificates (ML-DSA included), private and public keys (OpenSSH included), Diffie-Hellman parameters and PKCS#12 keystores — trying no password, the empty one and the Java default, and recording which opened the store — and writes on every certificate whether it is a certificate authority's (basicConstraints CA with keyUsage keyCertSign, lesson 28) and on every file which configuration files name it. It is in neither baseline, so the scanners-alone column is still exactly the tools. On the eight images it took 1 to 8 s each where theia took 75 to 136 s, and it is what closes the image layer from 14 of 20 to 20 of 20.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Covered: eight services and nine listeners (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, TLS behind PostgreSQL's upgrade, SSH), wire and image layers, pinned tool versions (testssl.sh 3.2.4, ssh-audit 3.9.0, cbomkit-theia 1.1.2) and the harness's own reader, on x86_64. The four-service numbers are from 2026-10-03.

Also covered, outside the slice and its answer key: Postgres, RabbitMQ and Kafka over TLS, a client-certificate listener, an ML-DSA-65 certificate, a client's offered groups, one Ruby rule — each tool on x86_64 and on arm64 under qemu-user emulation (spike S2).

Not covered: symmetric ciphers and MACs in a suite (the scan reads suites only for RSA key transport); CBOMkit's source scanners on real code (the key's five code-layer decoys are untested, the code layer is not scanned); Java keystores in JKS format (reported as unopened); UDP protocols; Zeek on arm64 (packet capture does not run under emulation); the M1 images under arm64. Arm64 results are from emulation, not a native arm64 host.

docs.title: What does a CBOM make possible once it exists?
The answer
docs.text: An inventory that is a list can be read. A CBOM whose entries carry their evidence, sit in a dependency chain and are rebuilt from a record can be used, in four ways a spreadsheet cannot be. It can be projected again into whatever field list is asked for, without a new scan. It can be compared with yesterday's to say what changed. It can be read against a policy to say what comes first and what blocks it. And it can be handed to a language model as the context for its work — which entry, on which listener, of which service, served from which file, with what evidence — so that a model can trace a weakness to the line that causes it and draft the change. The same entry is then what the result is checked against: a verifier probes the listener the entry names and decides, with no model in that decision, whether the change landed.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A model asked "make this database post-quantum" with nothing else will write something plausible about the software in general. Given the entry, it is asked something narrower and checkable: this listener at this address accepts these key exchanges, seen by this tool; the service's files are these; this line causes this one; this is the only file you may edit and these are the only lines that file may hold. The CBOM supplies the facts, the policy the intent, and the verifier the test. The model supplies the one thing none of them can: reading a configuration it has not seen before and writing the change.

That division is the project's measured position on models (note 13): a role goes to a model when a model reached a floor on it, and never the role of deciding whether a change worked.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
What the CBOM enables How Where it is shown Projection A field list is a data file; the record is rebuilt and projected in milliseconds the CBOM page, section 3 Comparison An observation's reference is its fingerprint; event references are left out the CBOM page, section 4; watch mode Prioritization The policy pack's rules over the entries and the owner's supplied facts the queues (note 07) A model's context The entry, its chain to the service, the service's files the trace and the draft, on each entry and each proposal Proof The entry's listener, probed four ways, on a copy before approval and on the estate after the change section (note 08)

The path for a service with no renderer. For software the harness can render by rule, a rule writes the change. For the rest, which is most of a real estate, the change-plan role drafts it:

  1. The context is the CBOM: the listener's entries from the latest scan, the investigator's trace where there is one, and the service's build files with line numbers.
  2. The model is told one file is editable — a policy file the service reads last — and which lines the runner will write in it. Three calls are made and all are recorded; the first usable reply is the proposal, with the model as its actor.
  3. The runner starts a copy of the service from the scope's image on an internal twin network with the proposed file, and the change's own check runs against the copy.
  4. Only a rehearsal that meets the intent opens the way to approval. A person approves; the runner applies, refusing any model's proposal that has no such rehearsal in the ledger and in its own log; the verifier probes the estate, the service is recreated, and the verifier probes again.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The records database, PostgreSQL 18 behind its TLS upgrade, holds benefits records with a 75-year lifetime. Its CBOM entries on 2026-10-21 (scan run 01M5FG9BJBCD7B6WNSM209P8XR) show it offering the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768 first and still accepting X25519, 2048-bit finite-field Diffie-Hellman and RSA key transport; its RSA certificate's key is the file /etc/pg-tls/server.crt. The queue rule placed its key establishment in the queue due 2030-12-31, not blocked on its supplier (PostgreSQL on OpenSSL 3.5 lists ML-KEM), with a validated module available and not in use. The investigator had traced the DHE group to the server's default — no live line sets it — on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL.

The policy for the listener was set to require. Gemma 4 31B on four L4s, given those seven entries, the trace and the four build files, drafted the same change in three replies of about 5 s each:

--- agency/generated/records-db/tls.conf
+ssl_groups = 'X25519MLKEM768'
+ssl_min_protocol_version = 'TLSv1.3'

The minimum protocol is what matters: TLS 1.3 carries no RSA key transport and no finite-field DHE. Rehearsed on a copy at 172.16.107.30, the change was enforced in 33 s: the hybrid-only client accepted, a client offering every classical group refused, the witness finding only X25519MLKEM768, and a TLS 1.2 handshake refused.

The counterexample is the plan that sets only the groups. On a copy with that file, a client offering every classical group over TLS 1.3 was refused — which, read alone, says "enforced" — while a TLS 1.2 client completed a handshake with DHE-RSA, and another with RSA key transport (lesson 36). A model that wrote that plan, or a person, would have been told it worked by a weaker check.

Two changes now wait for the owner's approval, in one change run (01M5FHSAWHMY78JV1EJX1YQA87 on the deployment): the records database's, drafted again under the scope regenerated that afternoon and rehearsed enforced in 37 s, and the jump host's SSH key exchange, which a rule renders into one line (KexAlgorithms mlkem768x25519-sha256) and which rehearsed enforced on a copy — an ML-KEM-only client agreed a key exchange, a client offering every other one was refused, ssh-audit found only the hybrid. A model drafts where spike S3 measured the role; OpenSSH had no change-plan items in the spike and needs no interpretation, so a rule writes it. Neither change has been applied to the estate.

docs.title: Where the CBOM sits in NIST's crypto-agility plan
docs.text:
NIST's white paper on crypto agility (CSWP 39-upd1, December 2025, updated June 2026) draws the plan an organization needs in order to change its cryptography repeatedly, as its Fig. 3. Crypto agility, in the paper's words, "describes the capabilities needed to replace and adapt cryptographic algorithms in protocols, applications, software, hardware, firmware, and infrastructures while preserving security and ongoing operations" (§1). The figure has five regions inside a loop: governance (standards, mandates, supply chains, threats, policies, stakeholders); assets (code, libraries, applications, files, protocols, systems); management tools that discover, assess, configure and enforce; data-centric risk management — an information repository feeding a risk analysis and prioritization engine feeding dashboards and measures; and the two outcomes it informs, mitigation and migration, which feed back to the tools.

A CBOM is that information repository. It is also what the other regions need from each other: the tools write to it, the engine reads it with the policy, the outcome is checked against it. The workbench's first page draws the figure, credited and with NIST's own labels, and fills each region with what the workbench does there, read from the ledgers at render time:

NIST region The workbench, on the mini-agency Who acts Governance OMB M-26-15 as a policy pack checked against the memo's text; the crypto policy; the owner's facts per service person, rule Assets services, listeners and images from the scans; call sites in one pinned repository scanner Management tools testssl.sh, ssh-audit, cbomkit-theia and the workbench's readers; rules; the runner; the verifier scanner, rule, model (the trace, the call-site read), verifier Information repository the hash-chained, ML-DSA-65-signed ledger and the CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM rebuilt from it rule Risk analysis and prioritization engine the queue, priority and blocker rules; conflicts settled by rule rule, model (explaining a conflict; a name the table lacks) Monitoring and measures the receipts: coverage against the key, changes landed, time-to-change verifier Mitigation items whose software cannot take post-quantum cryptography, marked for replacement rule Migration a change proposed, rehearsed on a copy, approved, applied and verified twice model (the draft), person, verifier

Each of the figure's labels is lit, half-lit or dim for the estate shown, with the reason, so the frame doubles as a gap analysis.

The figure also carries one weakness through the loop, step by step, as the ledgers recorded it. A scan finds records-db accepting X25519, 2048-bit finite-field Diffie-Hellman and RSA key transport. Rules link the listener to the service, and the owner's facts (a 75-year data lifetime, a high-value asset) attach to it. The OMB M-26-15 rules then put it in the 2030 key-establishment queue as a prioritized system. A model traces one finding to its cause, and a second model drafts the edit from the CBOM's findings and the files the CBOM links to the service. The edit is rehearsed on a copy, the copy is tried against each kind of client, a person approves, the runner applies it, and probes prove it on the wire twice. The next scan's CBOM shows the classical groups gone, with the signature queue still open, which is the plan's next step for the service. At each step the page says what the CBOM contributes. The models act in two steps of thirteen and never decide whether the change worked.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
• Build the record before the model. The model's work here is a few seconds; what makes it usable is that the question it is asked comes from an inventory with evidence and a chain, and that its answer is checked by something that is not a model.
  • Constrain what a model may write, not what it may think. One editable file, a fixed set of lines, a runner that refuses anything else. The model is free to read everything and to be wrong; it cannot write a line the service would load and the shape does not allow.
  • Rehearse before approval. An approver who sees a draft beside its rehearsal verdict is approving a measured result, not a model's suggestion.
  • Make the verifier stricter than the plan. The test that matters is the one the easiest wrong plan would pass.

docs.text: Covered: the mini-agency; one model-drafted change, for one PostgreSQL listener, rehearsed on a copy; the projection and comparison shown on the CBOM page. docs.title: How does a CBOM become a migration plan, and why can't a list of systems?
The answer
docs.text: A migration plan is an order of work, and the order is set by what the parts of an estate share. A certificate authority's new root has to be in place, and verifiable everywhere it is held, before any certificate it issues can move. Software that cannot take the new algorithms has to be replaced before anything that depends on it. A server is offered a post-quantum key exchange before it is required to use one, and required only when its clients can follow. A list of systems — the spreadsheet most agencies start from — names each system once and says nothing about what connects them. A CBOM records exactly those connections: which authority issued which certificate, which key sits on which listener, which build a service runs, what each listener accepts. From it, with the policy's deadlines, the order can be computed rather than guessed. Being able to compute the next change, and the one after it, from the record is what crypto agility rests on.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Three questions turn an inventory into a plan:

  • What depends on what. A shared thing has a blast radius: change it and everything tied to it changes too, or breaks.
  • What comes first. OMB M-26-15 prioritizes high-impact systems, High Value Assets, and data still sensitive in 2030. Among those, the longer data must stay secret, the sooner its key exchange matters: traffic recorded today is decrypted once the key exchange that protected it falls (harvest now, decrypt later).
  • In what order. The dependencies set a partial order; deadlines and priority break ties.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
The workbench computes the plan by rules each time it is shown, from the latest scan's ledger and every change run since. No model orders it.

Kind of dependency Found in the CBOM by What it does to the order Certificate authority a certificate file whose basicConstraints mark it a CA, and the issuer of each served certificate new root first, distributed to every service holding the old one; then every leaf Library build the runtime's own list of what it supports, per image, and which images share a build one service negotiating the hybrid group proves the build can: for the rest it is a setting Shared key the same public key (SPKI hash) served on more than one listener one step for all of them Clients' trust anchor a CA file the service uses to verify clients, issuing none of the estate's certificates the clients' migration sets the pace of the service's Supplier block the software lists no post-quantum algorithm for the function procurement, started now

Each step carries its deadline, the steps it waits for and unblocks, the CBOM entries it moves, the CBOM fields it was computed from, and its state: done when a change with the step's intent landed after the scan.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
On the mini-agency, eight services and the M-26-15 pack give 26 steps over 34 CBOM entries. Four dependencies tie them together, and 15 steps wait on another:

  • The internal CA issues the certificates of the records database, the message queue and the case-management application. The queue and the application run software that lists no post-quantum signature. So their replacement comes first, then the CA's ML-DSA root, then all three certificates at once. A plan that reissued each certificate on its own schedule would leave two services unable to verify their own chain.
  • The portal, the partner API and the post-quantum gateway run one OpenSSL build, on which the API and the gateway already negotiate X25519MLKEM768. For the portal the hybrid group is a setting, not an upgrade.
  • The API serves one key on ports 443 and 8443; reissuing for one leaves the other serving the old key.
  • The API also verifies client certificates against a partner CA whose keys its partners hold, so the partners' reissue sets the pace of its signature work.
  • The SFTP drop runs OpenSSH 6.6, which lists no post-quantum key exchange, while the jump host's OpenSSH 10.0 does: its first step is an upgrade the estate has already proved, not a procurement.

The records database's require change, applied and verified twice after the scan, shows as done.

docs.title: What if
docs.text: Any step can be taken as done and the plan recomputed: the steps it frees are shown. Taking the queue's replacement as done frees its TLS 1.3 step; taking both the queue's and the case-management application's frees the internal CA's new root as well. Nothing is recorded; the assumption lives in the address. It is how a planner tests which piece of procurement unlocks the most.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
• Plan from connections, not rows. The work that takes longest — replacing software, moving a CA — is invisible in a list of systems and unavoidable in a CBOM.
  • Start procurement now. Items no setting can move have the longest lead time and the same deadlines.
  • Measure clients before requiring. Every require is an order: offered, clients measured, then required.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Covered: the mini-agency, its supplied owner's facts, the M-26-15 pack, the capability snapshot of 2026-10-20. The dependency kinds are those this estate holds; others — a hardware module, a firmware root, a partner's own CA chain — are not modelled. Lead times are not estimated: "now" means only that the step depends on nothing else.
